title: Dodgers fans give Kyle Tucker an ovation, hoping to spark the struggling hitter’s bat
content:
LOS ANGELES — The latest attempt to resuscitate the worst season of Kyle Tucker’s career came before he even took a swing against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Friday night.

The first season of Tucker’s four-year, $240 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers has been an unqualified disappointment. Still, as he took his first at-bat against Pirates starter Bubba Chandler, the Dodger Stadium crowd largely cheered. Some stood and applauded, hoping to ignite Tucker’s quiet bat. They cheered when he went out to catch the first pitch. And again when his name came up in pregame introductions. And again when Tucker made a running catch to end the top of the first inning.

Nothing has worked this season. Maybe some positive affirmations could do the trick.

Anything is worth a shot at this point for Tucker, who started the night by hitting a 103 mph groundout to first base in the second inning and working a full count before taking a walk in the third. He entered the game with a .694 OPS, the worst mark of his career, and ranked 115th among qualified hitters with a 95 wRC+. His widespread woes, from his seeming inability to hit at Dodger Stadium to dropping a pair of fly balls in a week, have led people from manager Dave Roberts to the team’s own broadcast to wonder how much the struggles were weighing on Tucker mentally.

“I mean, it’s been a struggle in the sense that I’d like to help our team win and perform better for the guys in the clubhouse and the fans that come to the games,” said Tucker, who signed a deal this winter for the highest average annual value in Major League Baseball history. “In that aspect, I wish I would’ve done better this year.”

Still, Tucker maintained that he’s doing “all right,” and lauded the support of his teammates during the least productive of his nine big-league seasons. Roberts said Friday afternoon the four-time All-Star has “turned a corner” and “freed up” emotionally over the past week in hopes of recalibrating his season.

It would help to start collecting hits, particularly at home. Tucker has slashed .189/.286/.272 at Dodger Stadium, with a 55 OPS+ that makes him the worst home-ballpark hitter in the sport. His home struggles were so pronounced that when Roberts sat him last Saturday, he cited how Tucker was handling his home-road splits. He went 0-for-19 on that homestand, part of a career-long hitless stretch that spanned 26 at-bats until he doubled in his second at-bat Tuesday in Denver.

He was signed to this club to help boost a dynasty, adding star power to a lineup already coming off back-to-back World Series titles. Now, his struggles are a massive storyline in late August.

The Dodgers have worked with Tucker on his swing, with hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc saying this week Tucker “just hasn’t caught that … long hot streak.”

Roberts has shifted his emphasis with Tucker to the mental side of things.

“That’s what I’m locking in on,” Roberts said. “It’s a long season, tough season, every situation is different. For me it’s about kind of getting to the core of what’s going through his head.  … He’s not on an island. We’re here to support him.”

The keys, Roberts said, are “trying to get him to be engaging, knowing that they’re all in it together.”

Tucker tried something different Friday before any fans applauded him. Much of the outfielder’s pregame work has been confined to the batting cages. He has taken batting practice on the field a handful of times, dating back to spring training.

But when the group of primary hitters, including Max Muncy and Mookie Betts, finished their rounds, Tucker grabbed a bat and took his turn at the plate.

“I haven’t been hitting great this year, so I figured I’d try something else,” Tucker said. “Hopefully it helps.”

Roberts took this as a positive sign. Rather than fixate on his routines, Tucker was trying to tweak some habits.

“I think we’re all guilty at times of doing what we’re used to doing,” Roberts said. “So I think it’s just a good reminder for me, for everyone, that if it’s not working, it’s OK to kind of try something different and be a little uncomfortable. That’s not always a bad thing.”

Ultimately, it’s going to come down to results.
